kalmar.title: Physical origins of the Kalmár constant

kalmar-eq-12.label: Equation 12 · Kalmár’s theorem
kalmar-eq-12.description: The count of ordered factorisations across ranges up to x grows as a constant times x to the power ρ, where ζ(ρ) = 2.

kalmar-eq-15.label: Equation 15 · Capacity of organisation
kalmar-eq-15.description: The fixed charge per register sets a unique critical multiplier. With zero fixed charge, the multiplier returns to Kalmár’s constant.

kalmar-fig-1.label: Figure 1
kalmar-fig-1.description: Eight ordered layouts can hold the same sixteen symbols. The graph compares how many layouts exist for each range up to one million.

kalmar-fig-1a.label: Figure 1(a) · Eight layouts
kalmar-fig-1a.description: Each row groups the same sixteen ranked symbols into an ordered sequence of registers. The orange lines show the successive register boundaries.

kalmar-fig-1-caption.label: Figure 1 caption · Reference [1]
kalmar-fig-1-caption.description: The caption identifies the 2 × 8 and 8 × 2 layouts as the two panels in Figure 2 of The Cost of Complexity.

kalmar-table-1.label: Table I · Critical multiplier
kalmar-table-1.description: The critical multiplier falls as the fixed charge increases. The table gives numerical values from zero to eight units of fixed cost.

kalmar-fig-2.label: Figure 2 · The ensemble
kalmar-fig-2.description: The panels show the critical line, the number of organisations at a given budget and the mean depth of the ensemble.

kalmar-theorem-2.label: Theorem 2 · Structure of the ensemble
kalmar-theorem-2.description: Above the critical multiplier the depth is geometric. At each fixed depth the register ranges are independent draws from a power law.

kalmar-table-2.label: Table II · Organisation towers
kalmar-table-2.description: For sixteen symbols, the number of layouts falls from eight to four, two and one as each layout is itself recorded. Other ranges can end in a fixed point or a cycle.

kalmar-eq-31.label: Equation 31 · The reflective hierarchy
kalmar-eq-31.description: Theorem 4 gives the closure cost for a binary register at each reflective level as a binomial coefficient.

kalmar-fig-3.label: Figure 3 · The reflective hierarchy
kalmar-fig-3.description: The left panel compares the cost of closing organisation towers. The right panel plots the cost of a binary register at reflective levels one through four.

kalmar-limits.label: Outlook and acknowledgments
kalmar-limits.description: The draft describes its static model, identifies a branching prediction that awaits data, and records how the author and Claude developed the results.

cost-fig-2.label: Figure 2
cost-fig-2.description: Symbol 11 has two addresses among the same sixteen symbols. Each layout divides the choice between a register and a position inside it.

cost-fig-2bc.label: Figure 2(b, c)
cost-fig-2bc.description: Two registers of eight give symbol 11 the address (2, 3). Eight registers of two give it the address (6, 1).

cost-theorem-3.label: Theorem 3 · Equations 27–28
cost-theorem-3.description: When positional register costs add, repeated use of any fixed digit bounds the cost from above. The ratio of cost to log range approaches a limiting price per nat.

cost-theorem-4.label: Theorem 4 · Symbol cost
cost-theorem-4.description: The cost of reaching a rank is bounded below by the cost of its whole prefix. A positional construction with a terminator approaches the same limiting rate.

cost-geometry.label: Section III · The geometry of refinement
cost-geometry.description: The Hilbert curve divides a square into quadrants and visits them in order, repeating the division inside each. A rank names a quadrant, then a quadrant within it, down to a single cell, so each square is a register for the cells it contains and a symbol of the square above.

cost-width.label: Section III · Register widths
cost-width.description: Each square register is parametrised by its width alone, and a price for dividing it scales as a power of that width. The exponent of the price sets how the cost of refinement grows with depth, from constant through wall length to area.

cost-fig-3.label: Figure 3
cost-fig-3.description: The upper panel follows the Hilbert path through successive subdivisions, with the quadrant holding rank 11 becoming a register at the next division. The lower panel compares the complete cost under prices that scale as wall length, area and width cubed.

cost-fig-3a.label: Figure 3(a)
cost-fig-3a.description: The Hilbert path visits each cell once. The shaded quadrant contains rank 11 at depth two, and its cell becomes a register at the next division.

cost-fig-3b.label: Figure 3(b)
cost-fig-3b.description: The area-priced curve gains the same amount at each step, which is the logarithm. Wall-length pricing grows as a power of rank, and width-cubed pricing stays bounded.

cost-eq-38.label: Equation 38 · The cost exponent
cost-eq-38.description: The cost exponent depends on the dimension of the set and on how the price of a division varies with width. It fixes the whole cost function, and the number of children per division drops out of it.

cost-fig-4.label: Figure 4
cost-fig-4.description: The same rank order on four physical partitions: the Hilbert square, the Gosper island, the terdragon and the Lévy dragon. Pricing perimeters gives a power of the range whose exponent falls with the dimension of the outline, while pricing volume gives the same price at every level.

cost-fig-5.label: Figure 5 · Reading a perimeter
cost-fig-5.description: A Gosper parent divided into seven children. Short perturbations that change only the child address are blue and those that change the parent address too are vermilion, so the walls appear from address changes alone and the exponent is read from their fraction at successive depths.

cost-fig-6.label: Figure 6 · The guessing machine
cost-fig-6.description: The machine tests a candidate and halts on success. A failed candidate enters the reset ensemble before the next guess.

cost-eq-41.label: Equation 41 · The cost of a reset
cost-eq-41.description: For a complete classical reset, the heat bound depends on the uncertainty of the states entering reset and the initial temperature of the bath.

cost-eq-44.label: Equation 44 · The heat bound
cost-eq-44.description: Ordering the erased states by probability bounds their mean log-rank by their entropy. This gives a lower bound on the mean heat released on reset.

cost-eq-45.label: Equation 45 · Heat per attempt
cost-eq-45.description: The probability of failure weights the heat cost per attempt. The distribution entering reset is the distribution of guesses conditioned on failure.

cost-eq-49.label: Equation 49 · The rank distribution
cost-eq-49.description: A logarithmic price turns the maximum-entropy weight into a power of rank. Equation 50 gives the finite sum that normalises it.

cost-theorem-5.label: Theorem 5 · Zipf equilibrium
cost-theorem-5.description: For a finite register at fixed mean logarithmic cost, the maximum-entropy distribution is a power law. The mean cost determines the multiplier.

cost-fig-7.label: Figure 7 · The finite-cutoff Zipf family
cost-fig-7.description: Four panels compare rank distributions, response functions, partition sums and susceptibilities. The divergence occurs in the infinite-vocabulary limit.

cost-eq-54.label: Equation 54 · The infinite-vocabulary limit
cost-eq-54.description: With an unlimited vocabulary, the partition sum is the Riemann zeta function and converges for multipliers greater than one.

cost-weighting.label: Equations 57–58 · Weighted vocabularies
cost-weighting.description: A fixed weighting of the vocabulary changes the tail only through its growth. A weight that grows more slowly than any power of rank leaves the convergence threshold at one, a power weight shifts it, and exponential suppression removes it.

cost-fig-8.label: Figure 8 · The perimeter readout, all partitions
cost-fig-8.description: The measured fraction of finer-address changes that also change the coarser address, against the counted perimeter ratio, for every tested partition, with each case's deviation in units of its binomial standard error.
